screens.title: Capstone Project: A Complete IoT System
screens.narratorSegment: This capstone ties together everything you have learned: sensing with Arduino, edge processing with a Raspberry Pi, cloud integration, and a user dashboard. You will design a system that monitors temperature, humidity, and light, controls a fan and a lamp, and provides both local and cloud visibility. In practice this means assembling the hardware, writing Arduino firmware to read sensors and produce JSON, writing Python on the Pi to parse and timestamp data, storing measurements in SQLite, and uploading to ThingSpeak with retry logic when the network fails. You will also build a Flask dashboard for local control and set up basic security with HTTPS and SSH keys. A concrete example is the Smart Home Environmental Monitor: the Arduino samples a DHT22 and LDR, averages three samples, and sends JSON to the Pi; the Pi decides whether to run a fan or trigger an Arduino relay based on user-set thresholds. Common misconceptions include treating the Pi as merely a bridge — it is also an edge processor that must handle buffering, retry, and state. As you progress, think about how each layer contributes to reliability and visibility. What single test will you run first to prove your end-to-end pipeline works?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Capstone Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Capstone Project: Smart Home Monitor

Build a complete IoT system that senses temperature, humidity, and light; controls a fan and lamp; logs data locally; uploads to the cloud; and provides a web dashboard for monitoring and control.

In this lesson

You will design hardware, write Arduino firmware, implement a Python gateway with SQLite buffering, integrate with ThingSpeak, and build a Flask dashboard.

Coming up

Fault tolerance tests and a demo video that proves the end-to-end system works under network faults.

Explore Key Topics
Hardware & Wiring
Arduino sensors, relay and motor driver details you must wire and test safely.
Edge Processing
Raspberry Pi parses JSON, timestamps, logs to SQLite and applies thresholds for actuators.
Dashboard & Cloud
Flask dashboard with Chart.js and ThingSpeak uploads with retry when offline.
System Concept
Royal blue accents mean primary flow
Note: The Pi performs edge decisions, buffering, and cloud uploads. This avoids blind spots when internet fails.
Safety: Use motor drivers for fan control and observe relay voltage/current limits for the lamp.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this capstone you will be able to design a complete IoT system from a specification, assemble the hardware, write firmware and gateway software, and integrate with a cloud platform and local dashboard. Designing means producing a wiring plan and a clear data flow so every component has a defined role and failure mode. Building hardware means choosing wiring, motor drivers, and relay precautions, and testing each sensor and actuator. Writing firmware and gateway software means producing robust serial JSON, implementing averages and timing, parsing on the Pi, and logging to SQLite. Integrating with the cloud and a dashboard means implementing upload intervals, buffering when offline, and providing controls to change thresholds. For example, you will implement a three-sample moving average on the Arduino and verify the Pi stores rows in SQLite and uploads them every two minutes to ThingSpeak. A common misconception is that cloud alone guarantees reliability; buffering at the edge is essential. These objectives prepare you to deliver a tested demo, a project report, and a clear evaluation against the grading rubric.

screens.title: Verified Competency Milestones
screens.narratorSegment: These milestones map directly to the grading rubric and give you concrete checks to aim for. Second, the hardware milestone is a tested breadboard with each sensor producing plausible values and the relay switching the lamp safely. Third, the firmware and software milestone is verified by producing JSON serial lines from the Arduino and showing the Pi parsing and inserting rows into SQLite. Common mistakes are missing buffering or weak authentication. Each milestone helps you deliver a reliable, auditable project rather than a fragile demo. screens.title: Project Overview: Smart Home Environmental Monitor
screens.narratorSegment: Start by forming a precise project specification. The recommended capstone is a Smart Home Environmental Monitor and Controller that measures temperature, humidity, and light; triggers a fan and lamp; logs data locally; uploads to ThingSpeak; and provides a Flask dashboard for control. A complete specification lists hardware, sensing cadence, data formats, edge processing rules, upload schedule, security requirements, and acceptance tests. For hardware, the chapter specifies an Arduino Uno with a DHT22, an LDR, and a relay module; a Raspberry Pi 4 with Wi-Fi; a DC fan driven from the Pi via a transistor or motor driver; and an LED lamp on the Arduino relay. For sensing and data format, the Arduino samples every five seconds, computes a three-sample moving average for temperature and humidity, and sends JSON like {"temp":25.5,"hum":60.2,"light":450} over USB serial. Edge processing must add timestamps and compare measurements to user-configurable thresholds. A common mistake is underspecifying the data format and timing, which leads to parsing errors and flaky behaviour. Begin by writing a one-page spec that lists pins, sample rates, JSON schema, thresholds, upload cadence, and test steps. That single page will guide safe wiring, coding, and demonstrations.

keyIdea.title: Specification first
keyIdea.text: A clear spec prevents integration errors: list hardware, data formats, sample rates, thresholds, upload cadence, and tests.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Project Overview
System Requirements
  • Hardware: Arduino Uno + DHT22, LDR, relay; Raspberry Pi 4; DC fan via motor driver; LED lamp on relay.
  • Sensing: Read every 5 seconds; compute 3-sample moving average for temp and humidity.
  • Format: JSON serial: {"temp":25.5,"hum":60.2,"light":450}.
  • Edge rules: Pi timestamps, stores in SQLite, applies user-configured thresholds to control fan and lamp.
  • Uploads: Send to ThingSpeak every 2 minutes; buffer locally when offline.
Example acceptance test: With threshold 30°C, raise a heat source near the sensor until the Pi turns the fan on and ThingSpeak reports the temperature spike.
Data Schema & Timing
Use a single-line JSON object for each sample. The Arduino is responsible for averaging and emitting samples every five seconds. The Pi must accept that schema and add an ISO timestamp before storage. Explicit timing avoids drift and mismatched expectations between devices.
Why averaging matters: a three-sample moving average reduces sensor jitter, producing smoother charts and fewer false actuator triggers.
Common pitfall: unspecified units or precision. Always document whether temperature is Celsius and whether light is raw ADC counts.

screens.title: Hardware: Wiring and Safety
screens.narratorSegment: Hardware integration is about safe, testable wiring and choosing the right interfaces. For the capstone the Arduino handles sensors and a relay for the lamp, while the Raspberry Pi runs the gateway and drives the fan via a transistor or motor driver. Start with a wiring plan that lists each pin and expected voltage. For example, the DHT22 data pin to Arduino digital pin 2, the LDR to an analog input with a pull-down resistor, the relay signal to pin 8, and the motor driver inputs from the Pi's GPIO with a common ground. Use separate power supplies when motors may introduce noise, and include flyback diodes for inductive loads. A common mistake is driving a motor directly from GPIO — always use a proper driver and observe current limits. Test each sensor standalone: verify the DHT22 reports plausible temperature and humidity, and verify the LDR responds to light changes. Safety checklist items include verifying relay voltage rating for the lamp, isolating mains where necessary, and confirming grounds are common between Arduino and Pi for signal integrity. By building and validating each piece before integration you reduce debugging time and lower risk during final demonstrations.

keyIdea.title: Safe wiring is essential
keyIdea.text: Document pins and power, separate motor power, and validate each component before integration to avoid damage and flaky behaviour.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Hardware Integration
Wiring Plan (example)
  • DHT22 data → Arduino D2; Vcc 5V, GND common.
  • LDR voltage divider → Arduino A0 with documented resistor value.
  • Relay signal → Arduino D8; relay Vcc from 5V supply, common ground with Arduino.
  • Fan control → Raspberry Pi GPIO → transistor/motor driver → external 5–12V supply; include flyback diode and common ground.
Pro tip: use separate power supplies for motors to avoid injecting noise into the microcontroller power rails.
Testing & Safety Cards
Sensor Test: Read DHT22 values for 60 seconds and record plausible ranges before connecting to Pi.
Actuator Test: Use a multimeter to verify relay switching voltage and motor driver current without connecting mains loads.
Common Mistake: Directly driving motors from GPIO pins. This can damage the board; always use a driver or transistor with proper current handling.

screens.title: Arduino Firmware: Sampling, Averaging, and JSON Output
screens.narratorSegment: Firmware on the Arduino is responsible for sensor sampling, noise reduction, and producing a consistent JSON stream for the Raspberry Pi to parse. Define a clear loop that reads the DHT22 and LDR every five seconds, maintains a sliding three-sample buffer for temperature and humidity, computes the average, and prints a single-line JSON object. A concrete example is emitting: {"temp":25.5,"hum":60.2,"light":450}. Keep the JSON compact and stable to minimize parsing errors. A frequent misconception is to let the Pi poll sensors; instead prefer the Arduino to manage sampling cadence to keep timing predictable. Also avoid blocking functions inside sensor reads; if needed, use modest delays while preserving the timing guarantee. Test the firmware by connecting the Arduino to a terminal and verifying lines arrive every five seconds and show smoothed values. When you see occasional malformed lines, check for serial buffer overflows or excessive debug prints. Below is an illustrative Arduino-style snippet for structure; keep your real code annotated and include checks for sensor failures. End your firmware with a simple heartbeat or version string to aid debugging. Arduino Firmware: Sampling, Averaging, and JSON Output means arduino should own sampling cadence, averaging, and stable json output; test serial output before integrating with the pi.. In practical terms, read sensors, compute a 3-sample moving average, and send json over serial. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Arduino Firmware
Structure and key ideas
  • Sample sensors every 5s and store last 3 readings per measurement.
  • Compute a moving average to reduce jitter before sending.
  • Emit one stable JSON line per sample for the Pi to parse.
  • Include a small heartbeat string to detect firmware hangs.
Test tip: open a serial monitor at the target baud and confirm consistent one-line JSON records with no extra debug prints.
Illustrative firmware snippet
// Pseudocode structure for Arduino firmware
#include <DHT.h>
// setup arrays for last 3 samples
float tempBuf[3];
float humBuf[3];
int lightBuf[3];
int idx = 0;

void loop() {
  float t = readDHTTemp();
  float h = readDHTHum();
  int l = readLDR();

  tempBuf[idx] = t;
  humBuf[idx] = h;
  lightBuf[idx] = l;

  idx = (idx + 1) % 3;

  float tAvg = (tempBuf[0] + tempBuf[1] + tempBuf[2]) / 3.0;
  float hAvg = (humBuf[0] + humBuf[1] + humBuf[2]) / 3.0;
  int lAvg = (lightBuf[0] + lightBuf[1] + lightBuf[2]) / 3;

  // send compact JSON
  Serial.println(String("{\"temp\":") + tAvg + ",\"hum\":" + hAvg + ",\"light\":" + lAvg + "}");
  delay(5000);
}
This snippet is structural. In your firmware add sensor error checks and prevent noisy prints that corrupt the JSON stream.

screens.title: Raspberry Pi Gateway: Parsing, Timestamping, and Control Logic
screens.narratorSegment: The Raspberry Pi gateway serves three roles: parse incoming JSON from the Arduino, add a timestamp and persistent storage, and enact controls through GPIO. Parsing must be robust: accept one JSON object per line, validate numeric fields, and skip malformed entries while logging errors. After parsing, add an ISO timestamp and insert a row into SQLite for auditability and buffering. The Pi also compares current measurements to user-configurable thresholds set by the dashboard. If temperature exceeds the configured threshold, the Pi activates the fan via GPIO; if light falls below its threshold, the Pi sends a serial command to the Arduino to toggle the relay for the lamp. A concrete example: a parsed row becomes an SQLite insert with fields timestamp, temp, hum, light. A common misconception is to treat the Pi as stateless; but it must manage state for thresholds and ensure actions are idempotent to avoid repeated toggles. Test by running the gateway in a terminal and observe both S Q L inserts and GPIO state changes. Logging and graceful handling of malformed JSON will make later debugging far simpler.

keyIdea.text: The Pi must parse, timestamp, store, and act. Robust parsing and logging prevent silent failures and ease debugging.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Pi Gateway
Gateway responsibilities
Validate and parse JSON lines from serial. Add an ISO timestamp and insert into SQLite for history and buffering.
Apply threshold logic and control GPIO for the fan, or send serial commands to Arduino for the relay.
Buffer uploads and retry when internet connectivity returns to avoid data loss.
Debug tip: run the gateway in a terminal and watch both inserts and control outputs to confirm end-to-end behavior before adding cloud uploads.
Illustrative Python parsing and insert
# Pseudocode for gateway parsing
import json
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime

# assume serial_line is a single-line JSON string
try:
  data = json.loads(serial_line)
  temp = float(data['temp'])
  hum = float(data['hum'])
  light = int(data['light'])
  ts = datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
  conn.execute('INSERT INTO samples(timestamp,temp,hum,light) VALUES (?,?,?,?)', (ts,temp,hum,light))
  conn.commit()
except Exception as e:
  print('parse error', e)
Ensure the insert matches your SQLite schema and add retry-safe transactions for resilience.

screens.title: Serial Protocol and Arduino-Pi Commands
screens.narratorSegment: Reliable communication between the Arduino and the Pi depends on a disciplined serial protocol. The chapter prescribes the Arduino to emit one compact JSON line every five seconds with averaged values. The Pi should read line-by-line, parse, and acknowledge or ignore malformed lines. For control, the Pi may send concise commands to the Arduino to toggle the lamp via the relay. Define a minimal command language, for example a short ASCII command like SET_LAMP:ON or SET_LAMP:OFF, and ensure the Arduino acknowledges with a short OK or ERROR line so the Pi can confirm the action. A common misconception is expecting full duplex reliability without acknowledgements; always include simple handshakes for critical actions. Test sequence examples include: Pi sends a SET_LAMP:ON, Arduino replies OK, Pi logs the acknowledgement and updates the dashboard. Another test is injecting malformed JSON to confirm the Pi logs an error but continues processing. Logging, short acknowledgements, and timeout handling make the channel robust. Which simple acknowledgement will you add first to confirm actuations on your hardware? Serial Protocol and Arduino-Pi Commands means one json per line out of arduino; short ascii commands from pi with ok/error acknowledgements to confirm actuator actions.. In practical terms, stable json lines and simple command acknowledgements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Serial Communication
Recommended message flow
Arduino → Pi
One-line JSON every 5s: {"temp":25.5,"hum":60.2,"light":450}. Keep lines compact and predictable.
→
Pi → Arduino
Short ASCII commands for actuators: SET_LAMP:ON, SET_LAMP:OFF. Expect OK or ERROR replies.
Test: send SET_LAMP:ON; Arduino replies OK; Pi updates dashboard state.
Pitfall: no acknowledgement leads to uncertain actuator state. Add timeouts and retries.

screens.title: ThingSpeak Uploads and Local Buffering
screens.narratorSegment: Cloud integration gives you visibility and alerts, but the network is not always reliable. The chapter requires the Raspberry Pi to send sensor data to ThingSpeak every two minutes and to buffer data locally in SQLite when the internet is down. Implement a scheduler or timed loop on the Pi that batches or sends the latest sample at two-minute intervals. If an upload fails due to connectivity, leave the locally stored rows in SQLite and retry on the next interval. A concrete pattern is: insert every parsed sample into SQLite immediately, and in a separate uploader task attempt to send unsent rows every two minutes, marking them as sent only on success. ThingSpeak can provide charts and an email alert when temperature exceeds 35°C, so ensure your uploader sets the fields consistently. A common error is deleting local data on any HTTP error; instead, preserve rows and back off retries to avoid hammering the network. Logging upload attempts, failures, and successes will help you validate behavior during fault-tolerance tests. How will you confirm uploads resume automatically after a network outage?

keyIdea.text: Insert samples to SQLite immediately, upload every two minutes, and retry unsent rows so no data is lost during outages.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Cloud Uploads
Upload policy
Schedule uploads every two minutes. On each run, select unsent rows from SQLite, attempt to upload them to ThingSpeak, and mark rows as sent only on HTTP success.

  unsent = db.query('SELECT id,temp,hum,light FROM samples WHERE sent=0')
  for row in unsent:
    success = send_to_thingspeak(row)
    if success:
      db.execute('UPDATE samples SET sent=1 WHERE id=?', (row.id,))
  sleep(120)  # two minutes

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/api/latest')

screens.title: Security Practices for the Capstone
screens.narratorSegment: Security protects your device, data, and privacy. The chapter specifies using HTTPS on the Flask server with a self-signed certificate, TLS for MQTT or HTTP communications, a strong password for the Pi, and SSH key authentication. screens.title: Testing Plan: Fault Injection and Recovery
screens.narratorSegment: Testing and fault tolerance are critical to demonstrate a robust system. Follow a staged test plan: (1) test the Arduino standalone and verify sensor readings and JSON output; (2) test Arduino-to-Pi serial communication and confirm the Pi parses and stores rows; (3) simulate network failure by disconnecting Wi‑Fi and confirm the Pi buffers rows in SQLite and retries uploads; (4) send malformed JSON to test parser robustness; (5) test actuator commands and acknowledgements; (6) record a demo showing failure and recovery. For example, disconnect Wi‑Fi for five minutes while the Arduino continues to emit samples; after reconnecting, verify that the uploader sends the buffered rows and that ThingSpeak charts reflect the missing period upon upload. A common misconception is assuming immediate consistency in the cloud — buffering intentionally trades immediate cloud visibility for resilience. Logging is your best friend: log errors, malformed inputs, upload attempts, and acknowledgements so you can demonstrate fault-handling during grading. fullNarratorScript:
This capstone ties together everything you have learned: sensing with Arduino, edge processing with a Raspberry Pi, cloud integration, and a user dashboard. You will design a system that monitors temperature, humidity, and light, controls a fan and a lamp, and provides both local and cloud visibility. In practice this means assembling the hardware, writing Arduino firmware to read sensors and produce JSON, writing Python on the Pi to parse and timestamp data, storing measurements in SQLite, and uploading to ThingSpeak with retry logic when the network fails. You will also build a Flask dashboard for local control and set up basic security with HTTPS and SSH keys. A concrete example is the Smart Home Environmental Monitor: the Arduino samples a DHT22 and LDR, averages three samples, and sends JSON to the Pi; the Pi decides whether to run a fan or trigger an Arduino relay based on user-set thresholds. Common misconceptions include treating the Pi as merely a bridge — it is also an edge processor that must handle buffering, retry, and state. As you progress, think about how each layer contributes to reliability and visibility. What single test will you run first to prove your end-to-end pipeline works?

By the end of this capstone you will be able to design a complete IoT system from a specification, assemble the hardware, write firmware and gateway software, and integrate with a cloud platform and local dashboard. Designing means producing a wiring plan and a clear data flow so every component has a defined role and failure mode. Building hardware means choosing wiring, motor drivers, and relay precautions, and testing each sensor and actuator. Writing firmware and gateway software means producing robust serial JSON, implementing averages and timing, parsing on the Pi, and logging to SQLite. Integrating with the cloud and a dashboard means implementing upload intervals, buffering when offline, and providing controls to change thresholds. For example, you will implement a three-sample moving average on the Arduino and verify the Pi stores rows in SQLite and uploads them every two minutes to ThingSpeak. A common misconception is that cloud alone guarantees reliability; buffering at the edge is essential. These objectives prepare you to deliver a tested demo, a project report, and a clear evaluation against the grading rubric.

These milestones map directly to the grading rubric and give you concrete checks to aim for. First, your design milestone is a wiring plan and block diagram that lists each sensor and actuator with pin assignments and expected voltages. A concrete example: show the DHT22 data pin to Arduino digital pin 2 and the relay signal on pin 8, plus motor driver pins for the fan. Second, the hardware milestone is a tested breadboard with each sensor producing plausible values and the relay switching the lamp safely. Third, the firmware and software milestone is verified by producing JSON serial lines from the Arduino and showing the Pi parsing and inserting rows into SQLite. For instance, the Arduino should emit lines like {"temp":25.5,"hum":60.2,"light":450}. Fourth, cloud and dashboard milestone is evidenced by ThingSpeak receiving uploads every two minutes and the Flask dashboard showing a 24-hour trend and responsive controls. Common mistakes are missing buffering or weak authentication. Each milestone helps you deliver a reliable, auditable project rather than a fragile demo. Which milestone will you validate first when you build your system?

Start by forming a precise project specification. The recommended capstone is a Smart Home Environmental Monitor and Controller that measures temperature, humidity, and light; triggers a fan and lamp; logs data locally; uploads to ThingSpeak; and provides a Flask dashboard for control. A complete specification lists hardware, sensing cadence, data formats, edge processing rules, upload schedule, security requirements, and acceptance tests. For hardware, the chapter specifies an Arduino Uno with a DHT22, an LDR, and a relay module; a Raspberry Pi 4 with Wi-Fi; a DC fan driven from the Pi via a transistor or motor driver; and an LED lamp on the Arduino relay. For sensing and data format, the Arduino samples every five seconds, computes a three-sample moving average for temperature and humidity, and sends JSON like {"temp":25.5,"hum":60.2,"light":450} over USB serial. Edge processing must add timestamps and compare measurements to user-configurable thresholds. A common mistake is underspecifying the data format and timing, which leads to parsing errors and flaky behaviour. Begin by writing a one-page spec that lists pins, sample rates, JSON schema, thresholds, upload cadence, and test steps. That single page will guide safe wiring, coding, and demonstrations.

Hardware integration is about safe, testable wiring and choosing the right interfaces. For the capstone the Arduino handles sensors and a relay for the lamp, while the Raspberry Pi runs the gateway and drives the fan via a transistor or motor driver. Start with a wiring plan that lists each pin and expected voltage. For example, the DHT22 data pin to Arduino digital pin 2, the LDR to an analog input with a pull-down resistor, the relay signal to pin 8, and the motor driver inputs from the Pi's GPIO with a common ground. Use separate power supplies when motors may introduce noise, and include flyback diodes for inductive loads. A common mistake is driving a motor directly from GPIO — always use a proper driver and observe current limits. Test each sensor standalone: verify the DHT22 reports plausible temperature and humidity, and verify the LDR responds to light changes. Safety checklist items include verifying relay voltage rating for the lamp, isolating mains where necessary, and confirming grounds are common between Arduino and Pi for signal integrity. By building and validating each piece before integration you reduce debugging time and lower risk during final demonstrations.

Firmware on the Arduino is responsible for sensor sampling, noise reduction, and producing a consistent JSON stream for the Raspberry Pi to parse. Define a clear loop that reads the DHT22 and LDR every five seconds, maintains a sliding three-sample buffer for temperature and humidity, computes the average, and prints a single-line JSON object. A concrete example is emitting: {"temp":25.5,"hum":60.2,"light":450}. Keep the JSON compact and stable to minimize parsing errors. A frequent misconception is to let the Pi poll sensors; instead prefer the Arduino to manage sampling cadence to keep timing predictable. Also avoid blocking functions inside sensor reads; if needed, use modest delays while preserving the timing guarantee. Test the firmware by connecting the Arduino to a terminal and verifying lines arrive every five seconds and show smoothed values. When you see occasional malformed lines, check for serial buffer overflows or excessive debug prints. Below is an illustrative Arduino-style snippet for structure; keep your real code annotated and include checks for sensor failures. End your firmware with a simple heartbeat or version string to aid debugging. Arduino Firmware: Sampling, Averaging, and JSON Output means arduino should own sampling cadence, averaging, and stable json output; test serial output before integrating with the pi.. In practical terms, read sensors, compute a 3-sample moving average, and send json over serial. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Raspberry Pi gateway serves three roles: parse incoming JSON from the Arduino, add a timestamp and persistent storage, and enact controls through GPIO. Parsing must be robust: accept one JSON object per line, validate numeric fields, and skip malformed entries while logging errors. After parsing, add an ISO timestamp and insert a row into SQLite for auditability and buffering. The Pi also compares current measurements to user-configurable thresholds set by the dashboard. If temperature exceeds the configured threshold, the Pi activates the fan via GPIO; if light falls below its threshold, the Pi sends a serial command to the Arduino to toggle the relay for the lamp. A concrete example: a parsed row becomes an SQLite insert with fields timestamp, temp, hum, light. A common misconception is to treat the Pi as stateless; but it must manage state for thresholds and ensure actions are idempotent to avoid repeated toggles. Test by running the gateway in a terminal and observe both S Q L inserts and GPIO state changes. Logging and graceful handling of malformed JSON will make later debugging far simpler.

Reliable communication between the Arduino and the Pi depends on a disciplined serial protocol. The chapter prescribes the Arduino to emit one compact JSON line every five seconds with averaged values. The Pi should read line-by-line, parse, and acknowledge or ignore malformed lines. For control, the Pi may send concise commands to the Arduino to toggle the lamp via the relay. Define a minimal command language, for example a short ASCII command like SET_LAMP:ON or SET_LAMP:OFF, and ensure the Arduino acknowledges with a short OK or ERROR line so the Pi can confirm the action. A common misconception is expecting full duplex reliability without acknowledgements; always include simple handshakes for critical actions. Test sequence examples include: Pi sends a SET_LAMP:ON, Arduino replies OK, Pi logs the acknowledgement and updates the dashboard. Another test is injecting malformed JSON to confirm the Pi logs an error but continues processing. Logging, short acknowledgements, and timeout handling make the channel robust. If an upload fails due to connectivity, leave the locally stored rows in SQLite and retry on the next interval. A concrete pattern is: insert every parsed sample into SQLite immediately, and in a separate uploader task attempt to send unsent rows every two minutes, marking them as sent only on success. ThingSpeak can provide charts and an email alert when temperature exceeds 35°C, so ensure your uploader sets the fields consistently.
